chunks: And as for what Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Yahya ibn al-Mubarik from Abdullah ibn Jabala from Abu Jamilyah and Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked: 'If a dead person's head is cut off, what is due?' He said: 'The blood money (diyah) is due.' I asked: 'Then who takes its blood money?' He said: 'The Imam.' This is for Allah. And if his right hand or something from his limbs is cut off, the arsh (compensation) is for the Imam.'

key_terms.الإِمَامُ: The Imam, who receives the compensation in this context
key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: Blood money, full compensation for death
key_terms.الْأَرْشُ: Partial compensation for injury to limbs
key_terms.جَوَارِحِهِ: Limbs or joints of the body

ai.seo_question: Who receives the blood money for a deceased person whose head is cut off?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Istibsar clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between *diyah* (full blood money) for the head and *arsh* (proportional compensation) for other limbs of a deceased person, establishing that both are collected by the Imam. It reflects the Shia view of the Imam's authority in administering justice and financial rights even after death, distinguishing these post-mortem compensations from those applicable to the living. The narration underscores the systematic nature of Islamic inheritance and compensation law as interpreted by the Imams.
